en: The Tiantai Master Zhiyi said that "Gavāmpati" translates as "ox-chewer. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* refers to him as the "Ox King," and the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"In five hundred previous lifetimes, he was once an ox king; after an ox has eaten, it always..."
"His affairs are empty and his watchfulness is false;
as the retribution for his past deeds has not yet been exhausted, he constantly chews and crunches, and people of the time call him 'the ox-chewer'.

Long ago, there were five hundred geese, one of whom always obtained flowers and fruit to offer to the goose-king. When the Buddha accepted King Ajātaśatru’s invitation for the summer retreat, the five hundred bhikṣus all ate horse fodder, while Gavāmpati alone remained in the Śirīṣa Garden in the heavens, receiving the offerings of the Heavenly King.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states:
"Among those who delight in the heavens and do not delight in the human realm, the bhikṣu Goṣpada is foremost.
This "delighting in the heavens" refers to following one's own inclinations; it is the world-siddhānta (the conventional standpoint).
That which is brought about by the merit of making offerings to the king of geese is the human realm;
avoiding the laughter of men is the stage of remedial practice (*pratipakṣa*);
and that which is not laughed at by the gods is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and so forth.
It further states:

"People merely observe outward form and do not know of the presence of virtue; if one laughs at an arhat, one incurs sin. Because they avoid being laughed at by others, they constantly dwell in the heavens. The gods know of their virtue and do not laugh at their physical forms, and thus they reside in the heavens."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa convened a council of one thousand great arhats. He dispatched a junior monk to pursue Gavāmpati, who asked:
“Where are the Buddha and my preceptor?”
He replied, "All have ceased. He then said:
"The Buddha appeared and I appeared; the Buddha remained and I remained; the Buddha passed into extinction and I pass into extinction.
Thus the four streams of the Way flowed toward Mahākāśyapa. As he spoke these verses, it was said:
"When the great elephant has departed, the elephant calf follows; now that the World-Honored One, our preceptor, has entered parinirvāṇa, what more is there for me to do here?"
This is also the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the classification by teaching (*yōkyō*): dwelling in the celestial garden demonstrates good, while having the ox chew [the grass] demonstrates evil; this is the intent of the *Tripiṭaka*.

To attain the Way by chewing on one's own body with the mouth of an ox demonstrates that evil is not truly evil; to chew while dwelling in a celestial garden demonstrates that good is not truly good—this is the intent of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika*).
To demonstrate the good and evil within and beyond the realms is the intent of the Distinct Teaching (*pratiniyata*).
To demonstrate the true reality of good and evil is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Regarding "original and trace" (*benji*): the original state is to abide in the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*), dwelling securely as a holy sovereign, like a preeminent bull-king among the gods of the ultimate truth;
the trace is to manifest the behavior of a ruminant (*go-mukha*) while delighting in dwelling in the heavens.

Regarding the "Contemplation of the Mind": it is the contemplation of the principle of the Middle Way within the nature of the mind; proceeding with steady steps upon a level path, yet as swift as the wind—this is the "Bull King Contemplation" (*go-rāja-vipaśyanā*).
"Revata" is also called "Liyue"; this translates as "Constellation," or "Ursa Major" (*kṛttikā*), or "Provisional Conjunction. The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* refers to him as "Ever-Sounding."

Parents may pray to the stars for a child; once they have obtained one through such an invocation, the child is named after the star. Although he has left the household life, he still retains his original name.

Regarding "provisional conjunction," someone cites the *Śāstra* (Treatise): while staying overnight in an empty pavilion, he saw two ghosts contending over a corpse and informed them so as to adjudicate the matter.
"Whether I speak according to the facts or distort the facts, neither will avoid harm; therefore, I shall answer according to the truth.
The great ghost then pulled out his hands and feet, while the small ghost took the corpse to replace them. Having finished eating, they wiped their mouths and departed.
Because its cause is affliction and one cannot discern whose body it belongs to, it is said to be a "provisional combination.

Regarding the claim that it is always making sounds, one may doubt this matter: if it were my own body, I would have seen it with my own eyes being pulled out; yet if it were another's body, it still follows me in walking and staying.
Filled with doubt and hesitation, he asked everyone he met,
"Do you see my body? For this reason,
it is said that he constantly made sounds.
The assembly of monks said,
"This person is easy to deliver.
They spoke thus:
"Your body was originally the remains left by another; it is not your own.
Upon hearing this, he immediately attained the Way, and so forth.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Regarding those who sit in meditation and enter samādhi with minds that are not distracted or confused, the bhikṣu Revata is foremost.
In terms of the provisional teaching, this refers to the intention of the Tripitaka: to analytically deconstruct the five aggregates as not being one's own possession.
To realize that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally not one's own is the general meaning.
To discern that the ten dharma realms and the five aggregates are all not one's own is the specific meaning.
To realize that the five aggregates are neither one's own nor another's, and to perceive the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the aggregates, is the perfect meaning.
Regarding "original and trace": the original state is dwelling in the *Sūrya-tārakā-samādhi*, while the trace is the manifestation of this name.

Regarding "contemplating the mind": it is to contemplate the mind through mindfulness of the Buddha; seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions as numerous as stars at night when observing the constellations.
"Pingalavatsa" is translated as "residual habit. Having been a Brahmin for five hundred lifetimes, his residual pride remained high; as he was crossing the Ganges River, he said:
"Hey! [Stop!]"
"Little maid, stop the flow!
The river spirit divided the stream into two branches for him.
The spirit went to report this to the Buddha, and the Buddha ordered him to offer an apology; he immediately joined his palms.
"Do not be angry, little maid.
The great assembly laughed at this; she repented, yet continued to revile him.
The Buddha said:
"My practice has been such as this; truly, there is no pride in my heart.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"As for sitting in austerity beneath trees, avoiding neither wind nor rain, the Bhikṣu Vatsa is foremost."
Regarding the provisional teaching (*yōkyō*): the cessation of pride and the absence of pride is the meaning of the Tripitaka (*sanzō*).
That there is both pride and the absence of pride is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*tsūkyō*).
The differentiation of the high and low among the ten dharma realms is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*bekkyō*).
The eightfold mastery (*aṣṭavaśitā*) is the fulfillment of the Buddha-dharma; it is the perfection of the will.
Regarding the fundamental and the manifested: fundamentally, he dwells in the eightfold mastery of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, with a subtle and wondrous Brahma-voice;
as a manifested trace, he displays arrogance and harsh speech.
Regarding "contemplating the mind": it means contemplating how coarse speech and gentle words alike all return to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and so forth.

As for "Bakkula," this translates as "Fine Appearance" (*Sukhābhirūpa*); alternatively, it means "Noble Form," "Greatly Robust," "Fat-Bellied," "Lengdeng," or "Merchant-nature. However, because his physical appearance was upright and handsome, he is called "Fine Appearance."
He lived for one hundred and sixty years, free from illness and untimely death, having received the five rewards of immortality.

Although his stepmother placed him on a roasting pan or in a cauldron, or he was eaten by fish or cut with a blade, he did not die; because he had formerly observed the precept against killing, his life did not end prematurely for ninety-one kalpas.

"Because he once gave a single *harītakī* fruit to the Saṃgha in the past, his body is forever free from illness; he is able to uphold one precept and is adorned by four precepts, maintaining them firmly without violation even when avoiding neither fire nor water. While other people may uphold the five precepts, they mostly violate and break them," and so forth.

The body delights in tranquility and always dwells in seclusion, taking no pleasure in the midst of crowds; the eyes take no pleasure in colors such as black or yellow, the ears take no pleasure in hearing worldly sounds, and the nose does not smell worldly fragrances or stenches. The tongue has never spoken even a single phrase or two for others, and the mind remains constantly in meditative concentration without distraction—even toward the stūpas of the śarīras, it delights in quietude.
King Aśoka paid homage to the various stūpas of the arhats; next, arriving at one such stūpa, he spoke this verse:
"Though one may personally discipline ignorance, there is little benefit for the world."
He offered twenty cowrie shells.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"When he offered a single coin, cowrie shells flew out from the stūpa and alighted upon the king's feet."
The ministers were astonished and marveled, saying, "It is because he was secluded, possessed few desires, and even now that stupa still possesses such power.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"His lifespan was extremely long and he never died prematurely; he always delighted in living in seclusion and did not dwell among the crowds—Vakkula is foremost in this regard."
Regarding the provisional teachings: the *Tripitaka* (Śrāvaka) teaching is tranquility through the cessation of clamor to enter the Truth;
the *Common* (Pratyekabuddha) teaching is tranquility by realizing that clamor itself is the Truth;
and the *Distinct* (Bodhisattva) teaching is tranquility by departing from the two extremes to enter the Middle Way.
The center is precisely within the periphery; it is perfect stillness and quiescence.

As for the "fundamental," it refers to abiding fundamentally in the Great Samādhi of Quiescent Extinction (*mahāśānti-samādhi*). Longevity is permanence; freedom from illness is bliss; non-untimely death is self; and quiescence is purity.
Abiding in the foundation of these four virtues, one merely manifests through the traces of the six sense faculties their state of quiescence.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the nature of the mind is the Middle Way, which is simultaneously emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; it is the contemplation of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Mahākauṣṭhila" translates as "Great Thigh"; he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra, who had long excelled his sister in debate.

His elder sister was pregnant; when they debated, he did not prevail. Knowing that the one she carried had entrusted its wisdom to him through her eloquence, how much more so would it be once it emerged from the womb?
Having said this, he immediately left his home and went to South India, where he studied the eighteen scriptures.
The people of the time laughed at him,
saying, "What was difficult to achieve over many generations cannot be hoped for in a single lifetime.
He sighed deeply and said:
"At home, I am surpassed by my elder sister; on the road, I am held in contempt by others.
Vowing to study without ceasing, he had no leisure even to trim his nails; thus, the people of the time called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).
Having finished his studies, he returned home and asked where his nephew was;
people replied, "He has become a disciple of the Buddha.
Upon hearing this, he became greatly arrogant.

"My nephew, aged eight, has his fame resound throughout the five regions of India. What kind of spiritual arts does that śramaṇa possess to entice my sister's son? He went directly to where the Buddha was staying.
After reflecting for a long time, he could not find a single dharma to enter his mind, so he said to the Buddha:
"I cannot endure all dharmas; 'endurance' (kṣānti) means peace. This statement, 'I can destroy all dharmas,' means I can cause them to find no peace; therefore, I say I cannot endure all dharmas."
The Buddha asked:
"Do you see this patience?
This constitutes a position of double defeat.
If he had accepted the view of self, it would contradict what was previously stated:
"I do not accept any [view].
Since he did not accept the view of self and could thus not surpass the Buddha, he immediately lowered his head and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
When Śāriputra fanned the Buddha, he heard his uncle’s discourse and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"He attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); when confronted with difficult challenges, he was able to respond, being foremost among those such as Kauṣṭhila."
The Southern Heavenly King Virūḍhaka constantly comes to attend upon him. Regarding the provisional teaching (*yōkyō*):
externally it encompasses the four Vedas, and internally it encompasses the three piṭakas—the three piṭakas being the four types of eloquence (*catur-pratisaṃvid*).
"I have nothing to attain, yet my eloquence is such as this"—this is the eloquence of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
"Whether it be names or meanings, they pervade the ten dharma-realms"—this is the eloquence of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*).
The eloquence that relies on the true reality and pervades all things is the eloquence of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

As for "the fundamental" (ben), it refers to the fundamental abiding of oral secrecy (muk-mil) and the inconceivable transformation of the wheel of speech (muk-won), which are great meditative concentration (daedŭng) and great wisdom (daehye);
"the trace" (jik) manifests as the Great Knee (Daebi).
Regarding "contemplating the mind": to contemplate the mind is to see it as simultaneously empty and concentrated, simultaneously provisional and wise, thereby adorning the mind, and so forth.
"Nanda" is also called "Nanda the Cowherd"; this translates as "Good Joy," and is also translated as "Delight."
King Śuddhodana compelled one hundred thousand Śākyas to leave the household life; he was one of those very persons.
A certain teacher says:
"He is Upananda in this Vinaya."
Regarding the provisional teaching: that there is joy in phenomena but no joy in principle is the intent of the Tripitaka.
That the joy in phenomena is itself the joy in principle is the intent of the Shared Teaching.
The Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) refers to the Separate Teaching (Pratyeka-yāna).
The Abode of Joy (Pramuditā-vihāra) refers to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna).
As for "the fundamental," it abides fundamentally in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), being neither joyful nor not joyful.
The name of the stage is "Joy.

As for the contemplation of the mind: because one contemplates that the mind corresponds in a manner similar to the principle (*tattva*), it is called the "Contemplation of Joy" (*prāmodya-vipaśyanā*).
Regarding "Sundarananda": *Sundara* is translated here as "lovely" or "handsome," and *Nanda* is as explained previously; his lineage is as described in the section on Aniruddha.

He was born on the ninth day of the fourth month; he was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha, yet his countenance and deportment were so exceptionally distinguished that they differed from those of the world. If he entered a crowd, there were those who did not recognize him and said, "The Buddha has come."
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:

"In Magadha there was a naked ascetic who was of great intelligence; the people of the country called him 'the Wise One' and 'the Seer. When he debated with Śāriputra, he was rendered tongue-tied and a wholesome mind arose within him, leading him to desire to leave the household life and enter the Buddha-dharma."
Seeing that Nanda’s appearance was handsome and majestic, [the Buddha] remarked, "The wisdom of even a short and small bhikṣu is difficult to fathom; how much more so for one as grand as this?
Nanda was then ordained and left the household life.
The wife was Sundarī, who was exceedingly beautiful; they were never apart even for a meal or a breath.
As the Buddha and Ānanda were walking along the road begging for food, they arrived at her door. She was just then eating with her husband on a high tower;
she immediately rose to welcome the Buddha, but her husband said, "I must wait until you have returned before we eat together."
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How can one of the lineage of a Wheel-Turning King humiliate himself?
He then took the Buddha’s bowl and fetched some rice.
The Buddha then returned to the Nyagrodha Park and said to Ānanda, "Have Nanda bring some food.
Ānanda conveyed the Buddha's command, ordering him to deliver the meal to the Buddha. When the Buddha ordered his head shaved, he clenched his fist and said to the barber:
"Do not hold a blade over the crown of the King of Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha pressed him so insistently that he could not stop him, and thus he shaved his head.
The next day, when the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus were to accept an invitation, he requested to remain and guard the monastery, intending to flee.
The Buddha ordered him to close the door of his room and sweep the floor, opening it to both the south and the north to clean away the filth here and there.
Fearing that the Buddha would return, he immediately fled back home.
On the road he encountered the Buddha; he hid his body behind a tree, but the tree rose high into the air. Seeing this, the Buddha called him back.
He asked:
"For what reason did you leave?"
He replied:
"I parted from my wife yesterday; I am waiting for her return before eating.
I am merely thinking of my wife as she has gone."
"The Buddha is about to travel to heaven and hell," and so forth;
thus, it is marked with the character for "wife" (fù).

Regarding the classification by teaching (jiàoyuē): that there is the joy of the Dharma within the conventional truth (sùdì) but no joy within the ultimate truth (zhēndì) refers to the Tripiṭaka Teaching (sānzàngjiào).
That worldly joy is itself true joy is the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
From the joy of the Dharma of the Shared [Teaching], there arise worldly joy of the Dharma and intermediate joy of the Dharma; this is the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).
That the joy of the Shared [Teaching] itself encompasses all joys of the Dharma is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
The contemplation of the original and the trace regarding the mind is as previously explained, and so forth.
"Pūrṇa" is translated as "Fulfilling the Vow";
"Maitrāyaṇī" is translated as "Loving-kindness."
"Ni" means "woman.

Her father prayed to Brahmā at Manjiang for a son; it happened that the river was full, and he further dreamed of a vessel made of the seven treasures, filled with jewels, entering his wife's embrace. His wife conceived a child, and her husband's wish was fulfilled. Because all his aspirations were thus realized, she is called Man-wan (Full-Wish).
Her mother’s name was Maitrāyaṇī, which translates as "Compassionate Conduct" (Cixing) or "One of Knowledge" (Zhishishi).
This chapter exists within the four Vedas; because her mother recited it, she was named after it.
"Ni" (尼) means "woman"; "ni" is the general term for woman, while "na" (那) is the general term for man. Since he was born from Maitrī, he is called the "Son of Maitrī.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"My father’s name is Pūra, my mother’s name is Maitrī; thus, fellow practitioners of the holy life call me Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra."
He received his name from the two conditions of his parents; thus he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
This man was skilled in knowledge, such that there were no internal or external scriptures he did not know; because he was complete in his knowledge, he was further named Pūrṇa.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is foremost among those who are skillfully able to extensively explain and analyze the meanings and principles.
The subsequent passage says:
"He is the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
"Foremost" refers to the preaching of the full syllables (*pūrṇākṣara*).
Desiring to return to his own country to benefit others, the Buddha said:
"That land is corrupt and evil; what will you do? He replied: "I shall practice patience.

If they insult me, I shall consider myself fortunate not to be struck with fists; when struck with fists, I shall consider myself fortunate not to be struck with wooden staves; when struck with wooden staves, I shall consider myself fortunate not to be struck with blades; and when struck with blades, I shall consider myself fortunate to be spared from the poisonous vessel of the five aggregates."
This is called the fulfillment of the practice of patience; therefore, it is named "fulfillment.
As stated in the *Saptaratha-sūtra*:

"He is praised by the great wise Śāriputra; all fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) shall wrap their robes around their heads and honor him, and those who see him will obtain great benefit."
This is called "fulfilling through praise," and thus it is named "fulfillment.
Regarding the classification by teaching: to diligently analyze phenomena and have completed what was to be done is the fulfillment of the vow of the Tripitaka;
to realize that things are essentially empty and to attain realization within the dharma of emptiness is the fulfillment of the vow of the Shared Teaching.
The fulfillment of the Dharma-eye represents the fulfillment of the vows of the Separate Teaching;
abiding in the secret treasury represents the fulfillment of the vows of the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding "original and trace": the original vow has long been fulfilled, while the trace serves as the foremost in preaching the Dharma, manifesting to sentient beings the true nature of knowledge.
Regarding "contemplating the mind," it refers to the contemplation of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) such as those who practice the principles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

As for "Subhūti," this is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (*Kūṭastha*); at the time of his birth, all the granaries, treasuries, baskets, chests, vessels, and utensils in his home were entirely empty.
When asked by a diviner, the diviner declared it auspicious.
Because he was born from emptiness, he was named K'ung-sheng (Born of Emptiness).

His name was derived from the auspicious emptiness of the vessels and implements of his environment (*parabhoga*), using the characteristics of the external environment to designate the primary retribution (*mukhyaphala*) of the individual. Since both the environment and the individual were auspicious, he was called K'ung-sheng.
Because he constantly cultivates the practice of emptiness, he is called "One of Good Karma.
Because those who make offerings to him obtain rewards in the present life, he is called "Auspicious One" (Kalyāṇaka).

He always delights in dwelling and roaming in secluded forests, stone caves, and places of tranquility; the practices he cultivates take emptiness as their foundation. He constantly enters the concentration of emptiness and abides in the Samādhi of Non-contention (araṇā-samādhi); he rejoices in preaching the Dharma of emptiness, and whatever he explains or debates, he analyzes it all through emptiness.

He protected sentient beings so that they would not give rise to obstacles; when his walking meditation became tiresome, he would stop, and when his standing meditation became tiresome, he would walk.

When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, people from all over the land flocked together, vying with one another to pay him homage. [Mahākāśyapa] sat upright in a stone grotto, contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas: that form is not the Buddha, up to and including consciousness is not the Buddha; that the eye is not the Buddha, up to and including the mind is not the Buddha. Thereupon, he suddenly and brilliantly awakened to the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇī Padmā:
"It was not you who first paid homage; you paid homage to the form-body (rūpakāya), whereas Subhūti first saw the dharma-body (dharmakāya)."

Regarding the teaching by way of restriction (*yōkyō*): there is the arising of the wisdom that empties form, the arising of the wisdom that takes the essence of form as emptiness, the arising of the wisdom of emptiness from the wisdom of existence, the arising of conventional wisdom from the wisdom of emptiness, and the arising of the wisdom of the Middle from conventional wisdom. The arising of emptiness is itself the arising of the wisdom of existence; this is the arising of the perfect wisdom of emptiness, and it is this perfect wisdom of emptiness that arises here.
The "root" refers to the Dharma-body of the true mark of original abiding; the "traces" are manifested as arising from the perception of emptiness.
As for "contemplating the mind," it does not exist within, without, or in between, nor does it arise of itself; this is the Dharma-body of contemplating the mind.

“Ānanda” means “Joy” (Huanxi) in this language, or “Untainted. King Śuddhodana had hoped that his crown prince would become a Golden-Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakravartin) to rule over his realm; when the prince suddenly abandoned the kingdom and renounced kingship, the king’s grief was nearly fatal. Then a Māra came to deceive him, saying:
“Your son is already dead.”
The King wept and said,
"If Āyu’s words are false, then these auspicious signs must also be without efficacy.
Then another deity came and said:
"Your son has attained Buddhahood.
The king’s doubts remained unresolved; after a short while, a message arrived confirming the news:
"Last night, heaven and earth shook violently; the Prince has attained Buddhahood."
The king was greatly delighted and announced to King Śuklodana, "A son has been born.
The entire kingdom rejoiced, and for this reason he was named Nanda; this was the name his parents gave him.
Ānanda was so handsome that all who saw him were delighted; the Buddha therefore ordered him to wear a shawl to cover his shoulders.
Once, a woman leading her child to a well saw Ānanda looking at her with unblinking eyes, and unconsciously tied the rope around her child’s neck.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states:

"If the fourfold assembly hears what Ānanda has spoken—whether much or little—they are all without exception filled with joy. When they wish to pose a question, they first clear their throats by coughing, and the great assembly is filled with delight."
“If the fourfold assembly observes his silence, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, or his gestures, commands, advances, halts, and movements, they all rejoice.

Ānanda was born on the eighth day of the fourth month, the day the Buddha attained enlightenment; he has served the Buddha for twenty-five years. Calculating from this, the Buddha is fifty-five years old, and Ānanda is twenty-five.
At that time, the Buddha sought an attendant; five hundred [monks] requested it as previously described. The assembly exhorted Ānanda, and Ānanda complied. All five hundred were filled with joy.
Maudgalyāyana relayed Ānanda’s three vows to the Buddha, who said:
"Foreseeing censure and reproach, he requested not to accept robes or food; desiring his own benefit, he requested to have no fixed time for entering or leaving."
The Buddha approved and granted his permission.
The Buddha said:

"Ānanda’s service surpasses that of those in the past; while those of the past understood only after hearing the teaching, now, before the Buddha has even spoken, Ānanda already understands the Tathāgata’s intent, being fully capable of knowing both what is necessary and what is unnecessary."
Therefore, the Tathāgata joyfully entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda.

The Four Heavenly Kings each offered a bowl to the Buddha; the Buddha stacked them and pressed them together so that they merged into a single bowl, its four rims remaining distinct. This bowl was exceedingly heavy, yet Ānanda carried it with joy and without weariness.
The *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 7, states:
"Ānanda attended the Buddha for twenty-five years; of the eighty thousand *khandhas* he heard, he recited them all without omission, never asking about a single phrase twice."
With the power of mindfulness, he was filled with joy.

Ānanda followed the Buddha into the palaces of devas, humans, and nāgas; seeing the deva and human maidens and the nāga maidens, his mind remained free from attachment. Although he had not yet exhausted all residual thoughts, he was able to remain unstained, and there were none among the devas, humans, nāgas, or spirits who did not rejoice.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, while Ānanda was seated upon a lion throne, Mahākāśyapa and the great assembly praised him, saying:
"Your face is like the pure full moon; your eyes are like blue lotus flowers. The vast waters of the Buddha-Dharma have flowed into the heart of Ānanda."
He made a vow to sit and enter *nirvāṇa*, fearing that the Licchavis would harbor resentment if he remained, yet fearing that King Ajātaśatru would harbor resentment if he proceeded.
In the Ganges River, he entered the *vāyu-pracala* (wind-swift) *samādhi* and divided his body into four parts:
one for the devas, one for the nāgas, one for Vaiśālī, and one for Ajātaśatru.
King Aśoka paid homage at the stūpa of Ānanda, offering ten million taels of gold, and praised him with this verse:

“Because you were able to uphold the Dharma-body and serve as the lamp of the Dharma, the Dharma remains. Recalling the flourishing ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, I have thus established this supreme offering. Remembering how you maintained what you had heard much, your mouth issued subtle and wondrous words; you were praised by the World-Honored One and beloved by gods and humans.”
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"Ānanda is foremost in knowing the proper time, in understanding things clearly so that he has no doubts regarding what he encounters, in remembering without forgetting, in being widely learned and profoundly insightful, and in being capable of receiving and upholding [the teachings]."
Regarding the provisional teachings: Ānanda of Joyful Mind represents the Tripitaka;
Worthy Ānanda represents the Shared Teaching;
and Ānanda the Keeper of the Storehouse represents the Distinct Teaching.
Ānanda, the ocean is round. Regarding "original" and "traced":
the original state abides neither in joy nor in non-joy; the Dharma-body is like space, while wisdom is like clouds and rain, capable of both sustaining and receiving.
The outward manifestation is joy.

When one contemplates that the mind is identical with the semblance [of reality]—being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle—it corresponds to the contemplation of the mind as joyful; this continues up to its correspondence with true contemplation, and so forth.
"Rāhula" means "obscuration. In the past, he blocked a mouse hole and also did not look after a brahmin for six days; due to these causes and conditions, he is called "Obscuration."
The Crown Prince sought to leave the household life, but his father, the King, did not permit it. As he persisted earnestly without ceasing, the King said:
"If you have a son, I shall allow you to leave the household life."
The Bodhisattva pointed to the queen’s belly and said,
"Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son.
Because he remained in the womb for six years, it was called "obscured" (*āvṛta*).
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"Rāhu was originally named Asura; because he is able to use his hand to obstruct the sun and moon, this should be translated as 'the Obstructor of the Moon'.
The Buddha said:

"My Dharma is like the moon; this child obstructed me from leaving the household life immediately. He has obstructed me in birth after birth, yet I have been able to renounce him in every lifetime; therefore, he is called 'the obscuring coverer'."
After the Buddha had left the household life, Yaśodharā became pregnant. All the Śākyas were filled with resentment, asking, "For what reason has this happened?
They sought to punish her and even desired to kill her; malicious rumors filled the roads, though the noble lady Gopī’s testimony slightly mitigated the situation.
Because of the fire pit, he made a great vow:
"If I have done wrong, let mother and son both perish; if this is truly my remains, may Heaven bear witness!"

Because she had embraced her son and thrown him into the pit, the pit transformed into a pond, and a lotus flower supported his body; thus the king and the people of the country finally ceased their suspicions.

Later, when the Buddha returned to the kingdom, Yaśodharā had Rāhula offer a *modaka* (joy-ball) to the Buddha. Because Rāhula was of such tender years, he went directly before the great assembly to present it to the Buddha; by this act, Yaśodharā silenced the slander against her.
Because he slandered [the Buddha] due to having a son, it is said that he was obstructed by concealment.
The Grandfather King rejoiced, saying:
"Though I have lost my father, I have gained this son; as his grandson shall become a Golden Wheel-turning King, what cause for regret could I have?"
Anticipating that she would grow up, [the King] hoped for the arrival of the divine treasure.

However, when the Buddha requested that she leave the household life, the Father King did not permit it. Yaśodharā was about to ascend to a high tower when Maudgalyāyana flew through the air to fetch her; the Buddha then ordained her as a renunciant and entrusted her to Śāriputra to be his disciple.
Having already left the household life, he has also lost his royal throne; therefore, it is said that he is "obstructed.

Because Rāhula, while still a novice, was fond of speaking many falsehoods, when kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders came seeking an audience with the Buddha, Rāhula would answer them, saying: "He is not here."
"By preventing immeasurable people from seeing the Buddha, this constitutes obstructing others.
Because of this falsehood, the Buddha immediately rebuked him.

Upon returning from his almsround, he had Rāhula wash his feet; Rāhula held up the basin, turning it three times face-up and three times face-down, and then placed it on the ground and ordered water to be poured. Rāhula said:
"The water poured into an overturned basin does not remain.
The Buddha said, "You are like an overturned basin; within the Dharma of the Buddha, the water of the Dharma does not remain. Now you must speak the truth; do not speak falsely."
Later, when he practiced the path with diligence yet failed to attain realization, he asked the Buddha about it.
The Buddha said, "Have you ever explained the five aggregates to others? He replied:
"No. "Then you shall explain it to others.
Having finished speaking, he asked again, "Have you explained the twelve bases?"
"Have you not yet explained the eighteen realms?
To preach the Dharma is the gateway to attaining the Way; if you wish to attain the Way, you should preach the Dharma for others.
Because he spoke extensively on the Dharma and only attained the Way after that, this constitutes an obstruction.
Having already attained the Way, views and cravings are all eliminated, and birth within the three realms has come to an end; therefore, it is called "covering and obstructing.
Because birth in the three realms has ended, one can no longer be led by vows; therefore, it is called "covering and obstructing."
The Buddha commanded the four great arhats not to enter parinirvāṇa, but to wait until my Dharma has completely vanished.
For this reason, they remain in the world to this day and have not yet entered nirvana without remainder; thus it is said that they are "obscured and hindered," and so forth.
Regarding the provisional teachings: the Path Truth (mārgasatya) that analyzes phenomena to obstruct the four abidings is the intent of the Tripitaka;
the Path Truth that realizes the essence of phenomena to obstruct the four abidings is the Shared Teaching;
the sequential three wisdoms that obstruct the five abidings is the Distinct Teaching.
The threefold wisdom of the One Mind obstructs the five stages of dwelling; this is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Regarding "original" and "traced":

the original dwells in the Middle Way, obstructing the two extremes. Among the eight kinds of obstructions, those obstruct the side of *nirvāṇa*, while one kind obstructs the side of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Another kind is not an obstruction to birth-and-death nor an obstruction to *nirvāṇa*, but it obstructs the state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
The observation of the mind may be understood by analogy with what precedes, and so forth.
Sixth, the conclusion:

"Those well-known to the multitude"—some say that "knowing" (*jñā*) is simply "cognition" (*vijñapti*); others say that hearing the name is "knowing" and seeing the form is "cognition"; or that seeing the form is "knowing" and seeing the mind is "cognition."
The "fundamental" refers to acting as a teacher of the full syllables for the sake of sentient beings, while the "traces" refer to acting as a teacher of the half-syllables, and so forth.
The knowledge of contemplative practice is like that of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Having concluded the section on those with extensive knowledge, the next lists those with limited knowledge:

"Furthermore, there were two thousand [monks], both learners and those beyond learning. This merely cites their status and number without praising their virtues; thus, they are referred to as the assembly of those with limited knowledge.

The Sage has severed ties with both the holy and the mundane, nor does he discriminate between those of great learning and those of little learning. He specifically employs extensive knowledge to guide those who aspire to the lofty and admire the distant, and employs limited knowledge to guide those who conceal their names, hide their virtues, and practice humility. Because he accords with sentient beings, there appear to be various distinctions; yet one must not lose sight of his fundamental essence due to these outward traces of much or little learning.
Regarding "those in training and those beyond training": within the Tripiṭaka, there are eighteen types of persons in training (*śaikṣa*) and nine types of persons beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), those in the first five stages are called "in training," while the sixth stage is called "beyond training. Furthermore, in the Shared Teaching, those in the [first] nine stages are termed "in training," and the Buddha-stage is termed "beyond training.

Within the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (*bhūmi-yāna*), "training" and "beyond training" are clarified either in terms of effortful practice versus effortless spontaneity, or in terms of being fully accomplished versus not yet fully accomplished.
The *Āgama* states:
"A non-Buddhist asked the Buddha:
'Does an Arhat still study further?'"
The Buddha said:
"An Arhat does not perform unwholesome dharmas and abides in wholesome dharmas; one who trains in that which is beyond training is called 'one in training' (śaikṣa).
If this is so, then those still in training would also be termed "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
When a trainee (śaikṣa) has completed what was to be abandoned and no longer has further abandonment to perform, they are one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa); these constitute four categories.
Regarding the five preliminary practices (pañca-upāya), those that are neither trainee nor beyond training constitute five categories.
By analogy with the four teachings, it should also be understood in this way; thus there are twenty phrases, comprising four sets of five.

Regarding the "Original" and the "Traces": the Original refers to the Great Being of the Dharma-body, who dwells in the stage of No-More-Learning within the study of the *maṇḍala* (full) letters. As for sentient beings, they should perceive him as one who has attained the stage of No-More-Learning through the study of the *ardha* (half) letters, thereby adorning the twin trees.

The observer correctly contemplates the Middle Way, not relying on the two extremes; that which is between them is the state of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa), and one who can contemplate in this manner is called a learner (śaikṣa).

If we clarify the numerical categories according to the gate of contemplation: contemplating the ten Dharma-realms and the ten suchnesses within form and mind—when these realms and suchnesses are discussed in relation to one another—they total two thousand. Because the traces are brought forward, the fundamental reality is indicated; thus, the trace is itself the fundamental trace.
Regarding the subsequent listing of the community of nuns: previously, this was categorized as two groups following the preceding example, but that is no longer accepted.
If one were to categorize them as two groups—the highly learned and the less learned—following the preceding example, there is again no scriptural authority for it, nor is it logically tenable.
However, since we are merely citing the leaders of the two assemblies, why must we laboriously designate them as "great" and "small," or "many" and "few"?
First, "Prajāpatī" is listed; this translates as "Mahāmāyā" (Great Love-Path), or alternatively as "Kautamī," which translates as "Leader of the Assembly. "Nī" is a general term for women in India.
The Dharma-gate of the Fundamental Abiding Prajñāpāramitā serves as the trace of the mother of the thousand Buddhas, giving birth to the Teachers.
Regarding the commentator: "Mādhyamika" is called "Great" because it is vast and extensive;
"unconditioned compassion" is called "Love."
The central principle of empty penetration is called the Way (*mārga*).
"Great" refers to one's own practice;
"affection" refers to transforming others—just as one undergoes birth because of affection, and enters into the realm of existence because of compassion.
The Way consists of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
"Six thousand" refers to a number.

Regarding the "gate of contemplation," it means contemplating that the purity of the six sense organs possesses a thousand merits; although the eyes have eight hundred and the ears twelve hundred, since the greater complements the lesser, the total reaches six thousand, symbolizing the fundamental Dharma-gate and representing the intent of contemplative practice.

Regarding "Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula": she is designated by her son; this name translates as "Flower Color" (Huase), is also called "Renown" (Mingwen), or is said to have no literal equivalent. Her virtue of gentleness, kindness, propriety, and frugality was equal to that of the Prince. While at home, she was the wife of the Bodhisattva and a spiritual friend to devas and humans; after leaving home, she became the leader of the community of nuns and attained the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa). How could she not possess great renown?
The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* mentions three consorts:
first, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; and third, Mṛgajā.
Both the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya* and the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* state that Rāhula was the son of Gopī.
Both the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* state that he was the son of Yaśodharā.
How can these two meanings be reconciled?
It may be that those sūtras refer to the mother, while this passage refers to the one born from her.
The *Śāstra* states that Gopī was a precious woman who was barren;
she is none other than Gopī, which translates as "Bright Woman. Thus, it is certain that she is the mother of Yaśodharā.
Regarding the "original" and the "traced": as for his wife, she was Qi. How could one of such vast virtue be the wife of a crown prince?
Thus we know that while he originally dwelt in the subtle joy of the Dharma within tranquil concentration, he appeared in the traced form as the Buddha’s wife.
The *Karunāpuṣpa* states:
"At the abode of the Buddha Ratnagarbha, she vowed to become his wife.
Contemplating emptiness and the joy of the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, she then used the Deer Park to symbolize his wife.
Observing the provisional path of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and its dharma-joy, Yaśodharā is used to represent the wife;
observing the middle [truth] and its dharma-joy, Gopī is used to represent the wife.

Above, it was clearly explained through the original and the manifested (*honjaku*), and through the contemplation of the mind; now, this is further discussed in general to reveal the subtle ingenuity of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and to clarify the subtlety of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
Now, the various manifestations of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi adapt to the capacities of sentient beings without exception;
let us discuss this briefly from a proximate perspective. He took his station in the royal palace and descended as a spirit into the Holy Queen.

As for the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas, they all assist the Buddha in his transformative work, casting their reflections into other families. Thus, amidst the thirty-two auspicious omens, his golden form was born in response to the world. All...
The Great Beings each manifested their births: some caused jewels to rain from empty rooms, while others employed eloquence to communicate through dreams.
Just as the Imperial Prince abandoned his kingdom and renounced his kingship to scale the city walls and study the Way, so too did all these Great Beings request instruction from their teachers;
they mastered both talent and artistry to become masters of their respective schools, like the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma that brings the nectar of immortality.
When the gate opens, one hears that the great beings (mahāsattvas) have not yet matured their conditions for transformation;

thus they manifest as if they do not accept [the teachings], meeting them with equal courtesy to honor the truth of our Way. In this state, the transformer and the transformed both preserve their original nature like milk.

However, when the conditions for those to be transformed have matured, they are like plain silk easily dyed, or like lotuses blooming early in the pond; the ordinary is transformed into the sacred, and milk is turned into curd.

The Master’s school regards him as the foremost disciple of the Buddha, being first among those preeminent in wisdom, supernatural powers, eloquence, or samādhi; together they assist the Dharma King to further deliver those not yet delivered and to bring to full maturity those already matured. At the assembly for the Vaipulya sūtras, hearing of the inconceivable merit of the Bodhisattvas, he felt ashamed of the Small Vehicle and yearned for the Great. Feeling shame for the Small, he sighed in self-reproach, lamenting that he had lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision; yearning for the Great, he did not know how he might attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom, like transforming curd into fresh butter.

Next, one hears the gate of the Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā, which begins with the investigation of form and mind and culminates in the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). It encompasses both the Small and Great Vehicles, involving inclusion and exclusion, taking and giving, whether shared or distinct, partial or complete. One receives and understands these instructions without seeking personal gain; though not yet abandoning [delusions] all at once, one gradually becomes clear and unobstructed, like transforming raw butter (*sarpis*) into refined butter (*ghṛta*).

Next, one hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which harmonizes the nature of the Dharma, establishes the father-son relationship, bestows predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), and entrusts the Mahāyāna. It abolishes the three vehicles and returns them to the One, just as the other four flavors ultimately become the same single *amṛta* (clarified butter). It does not allow even a single person to attain extinction alone, but rather causes all to attain extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.

The Dharma King and his Dharma ministers appear in the world for a great purpose, skillfully employing expedient means: first using the "half-syllable" teachings to clear away the overgrown thickets of the twenty-five states of existence, thereby establishing the four withered trees and twin *śāla* trees to benefit sentient beings.

Next, by employing the method of "half and full," one breaks the solitary goodness of the two vehicles and accomplishes the vastness of the Bodhisattvas, thereby achieving the four glories and the dual trees to benefit the sages.

Subsequently, by employing the eternally abiding *pūrṇākṣara* (full syllable), he breaks through the temporal sequence of the two extremes, thereby perfecting the Buddha’s secret treasury—which is neither withered nor flourishing—and bringing ultimate benefit.

Having completed the merit of his leadership and fulfilled his great vows, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana ceased their transformative activities within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The Holy Lord redeemed their lives, yet this too was not for long; as the text says:
"According to my original vow, it is now fulfilled; the Tathāgata shall before long enter *nirvāṇa*."

The proclamation of "nirvana" originated from this; the twenty thousand Buddhas, such as Dīpaṃkara and Kāśyapa, all reached their ultimate consummation in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Now, since both teacher and disciple have revealed their origins through this sūtra, they secretly conceal the Bodhisattva path within while outwardly manifesting as śrāvakas.

"I have indeed been a Buddha for immeasurable billions of kalpas"—inferring from this, we see that the great Arhats, from the ground of the Dharmakāya, cast their reflections and follow conditions as traces appearing before the myriad waters; they manifest as those in training and those beyond training, as men and as women, showing the Way to both monastics and laity. Through the power of Śūraṅgama, there is nothing they do not manifest; such is the nature of their skillful means and expedient wisdom, and so forth.

Regarding the general explanation of contemplation: this is that which the Master and Disciple perform as the transformative activity of the Dharmakāya. If one does not employ the skillful means of contemplation, it will be of no benefit to the practitioner—like a poor person counting treasures, or like a blind man holding a candle.

However, mental factors (*caitasika*) are exceedingly numerous; for now, we shall take the wholesome ones as an illustration. Just as among many disciples only ten are selected, so too regarding the ten wholesome mental factors—namely:

faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and ethical discipline (*śīla*)—these ten factors assist the King of the Mind (*citta-rāja*). They are able to transform evil into good and change the mundane into the sacred, accomplishing all dharma-gates. Taking these ten mental states as the foundation is like having ten disciples who assist the Buddha in his transformative work, collectively maturing sentient beings and establishing them in the Buddha-dharma.

Faith corresponds to the number one, and Aniruddha is foremost among those with the divine eye; the eye is the head of the five faculties, just as the east is considered the superior direction among all quarters. Thus, faith is the first entry into the Buddha-dharma among all the numerical categories.
The application of energy (*vīrya*) corresponds to Kāśyapa, who was foremost among those who practice asceticism (*dhūta*); "shaking off" through diligent austerity is the application of energy.

The application of mindfulness (*smṛti*) corresponds to Upāli, who was foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya; the power of mindfulness is firm and strong, characterized by the ability to remember and maintain [the teachings] without forgetfulness.

The category of concentration corresponds to Maudgalyāyana, who is foremost in supernatural powers; the category of wisdom corresponds to Śāriputra, who is foremost in wisdom—both of these can be easily understood.
The category of joy corresponds to Ānanda, who is foremost in erudition (*bahuśruta*). To distinguish the categories: joy is precisely the category of joy.

In his discourse with Citta-ātreyaputra, the Master relied on numerical categories to discuss the essence of phenomena, exhausting their subtleties and exhausting their principles; he eliminated the heterodox and revealed the orthodox, just as one relies on the abandonment of evil to attain good, or the relinquishing of suffering to enter into bliss.
Śāriputra, foremost in understanding emptiness, corresponds to the faculty of equanimity; if one abides in the equality of emptiness, it accords with the faculty of equanimity.
Pūrṇa, foremost in preaching the Dharma, corresponds to the faculty of discernment; since discernment is the root of speech, when this root is established, eloquent exposition becomes inexhaustible.
It can be understood that among those who count their precepts, Rāhula was foremost in maintaining them.

The ten counts support the mind-king and enable the accomplishment of contemplative practice; within a single thought-moment, one enters deeply into wholesome dharmas. The Three Jewels are fully present therein: the "King" is the Buddha Jewel;
the "counts" are the Sangha Jewel.
The actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as its object-condition is neither king nor number; it is the Dharma-jewel.
If one enters the merit of the king and numbers within actual reality, its functional power is sufficient.
Furthermore, taking the ten numbers that pervade the great earth, they arise together with the mind-king, entering into both good and evil and pervading all things, namely:
These are perception, desire, contact, wisdom, mindfulness, volition, liberation, recollection, concentration, and feeling.
Regarding perception, Pūrṇa has attained its conventional designation; he is well-versed in conventional designations, and his eloquence is unimpeded.
When he wished to engage with Kāśyapa, Kāśyapa was free from worldly desires and sought the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

When he engaged with Candra-kumāra-bhūti (Candana), the two matters of contact and entry were mutually interpenetrated; Candana was skilled in debating principles and could exhaustively pursue the dialogue back and forth.
"Wisdom" refers to Śāriputra, which is easily understood.
"Mindfulness" corresponds to Upāli; mindfulness is the supreme means for upholding the Vinaya.
"Contemplation" corresponds to Rāhula; contemplation is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and this person truly practices and maintains the precepts.
Liberation corresponds to Śubhavyūha; "liberation" means being free from entanglements, as this person understands emptiness and attains liberation within existence.
Mindfulness corresponds to Aniruddha; mindfulness involves movement and the grasping of objects to cultivate the divine eye, which easily brings about samādhi.
The fixed number [of disciples] corresponds to Maudgalyāyana, who can be understood through his supernormal powers.
Their reception [into the order] corresponds to Ānanda, for his extensive learning and retention are free from error.

Each of these ten individuals is endowed with a multitude of virtues; they serve as leaders in their respective specialties to proclaim the Buddha-way according to the inclinations of sentient beings.

Those who desire wisdom take Śāriputra as their teacher, and even those who desire extensive learning take Ānanda as their teacher; together they assist the Dharma King, each presiding over a specific office. Now, observing the mind is also like this:

within each and every moment of mind, all the mental factors (caitasikas) are fully present. For the sake of accomplishing contemplation, these mental factors support one another to bring about awakening—whether one enters the Path through the factor of perception (saṃjñā) or through the factor of desire (chanda). According to what is appropriate, the mind-king and the mental factors work together to subdue them, transforming the various minds of worldly afflictions (kleśa) into the work of a Buddha.
When one practices this contemplation but has not yet attained awakening, the practice is like milk;
if one gives rise to outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), the practice is like curd;
if one shatters the dust-like afflictions, it is like fresh or refined clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
If one destroys ignorance and contemplates [reality] as being like clarified butter (sarpis),

and upon reaching the stage of clarified butter (ghṛta) all kingly enumerations are exhausted— because the enumerations of mind and mental factors no longer function— one is said to be practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.
The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"Contemplate the mind as being without mind; phenomena do not abide in phenomena. My own mind is naturally empty, and thus neither sin nor merit has a master.
This state of no-mind and no-number is called right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
If these mental afflictions (*kleśa*) are not exhausted, then contemplation will never reach its conclusion; therefore, the Sūtra says:
"As long as sentient beings have not been delivered, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment."
This is precisely that meaning, and so forth.
Regarding the second point, the listing of the assembly of bodhisattvas, the *Vyākhyā* states:
"Bodhisattvas are subsumed within the fourfold assembly of both the ordained and the laity; for what reason are they listed separately?"
Answer:

"There are bodhisattvas who fall among the fourfold assembly, yet there are members of the fourfold assembly who do not fall among the bodhisattvas; because they have not resolved to become Buddhas, they are now listed separately."
Those who have likewise resolved their minds to seek Buddhahood are called the assembly of bodhisattvas.
The text consists of six parts;
the first is their common nature.
2. The Great Number; 3. The Stages;
4. The Praise of Virtues.
V. Listing the names;
VI. Concluding statement.
First, regarding "those of similar category," these are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
If it were preserved in full, one should say *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*; Master Kumārajīva, finding it cumbersome, abbreviated it by omitting the two characters *sattva*.
*Bodhi* here means "Way" (*mārga*);
*sattva* here means "mind" (*citta*).
"Mahā" means "great. These individuals all seek the vast and expansive Great Way;
furthermore, because they bring sentient beings to maturity, they belong to the same category as those with the aspiration for enlightenment and the mind of the Great Way.

There are many kinds of bodhisattvas, namely those of the partial (p’ien), the common (t’ung), the distinct (pieh), and the perfect (yüan). For example, when the *Śāstra* cites Kātyāyanīputra’s explanation that one fulfills the six perfections by reaching their respective limits, this is intended to refine blood into milk for sentient beings.
If the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* explains that there are bodhisattvas whose resolve corresponds to *sarvajñatā*, this is intended to refine milk into curd.

If the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* explains that there are bodhisattvas who resolve to sport with supernatural powers and purify buddha-lands, or as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, those who have attained inconceivable liberation and are able to manifest transformed bodies, ascend thrones, and yet again submit to being humbled and rebuked, this is intended to refine curd into fresh and refined butter.

If the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that there are bodhisattvas who, upon generating the mind of enlightenment, immediately sit beneath the Bodhi tree, attain perfect awakening, and turn the wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings, this is like refining curd into the finest ghee (*amṛta*).
Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"When the Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed.
It further states:
"If a bodhisattva does not hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they are not practicing the bodhisattva path well; if they hear this sutra, they are practicing the bodhisattva path well.
Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"If a bodhisattva does not hear the *Nirvāṇa*, they will always harbor expectations."
If one hears the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, all hopes and expectations come to rest. Thus, there are briefly four kinds [of teachings].

Regarding the fundamental and the manifested (*honji* and *jakuji*): the fundamental ground is difficult to fathom; they may dwell at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) or be equal to the Dharma King. This is like Sudhana entering the Dharma-realm and beholding Mañjuśrī’s form and appearance as boundless, and his Dharma-gates as profound and far-reaching. Fundamentally, they are neighbors to the Buddhas; manifestly, they assist Śākyamuni as Bodhisattvas. By the power of the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms, they project their reflections and display their countenances, using the inconceivable Wheel of Speech to preach extensively according to what is appropriate. This can be known by the mind, but cannot be fully debated through words.

Therefore, the traces of the four flavors are led back to the single reality. This is like using a hammer and an anvil to refine various raw materials; once the *sarpis* (clarified butter) has been perfected, the period of transformation comes to rest. Yet, as for the ultimate accomplishment of its original ground, how could it be that one only enters the Mahāyāna today?

Nor is it that the high mountain of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) shines first; whether sudden or gradual, these are all merely manifestations of the traces [of the teaching]. As for "contemplative understanding" (*guānjiě*):

contemplating the mind through the Middle Way while simultaneously illuminating the two truths is called "Great" (*dà*); penetrating to the fruit of Bodhi is called the "Way" (*dào*); and destroying the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the five abodes is called "accomplishing sentient beings," and so forth.
"Eighty thousand people" refers to the number.
Since the assemblies in other sutras are very large, why is this sutra so small?
Perhaps it expresses a general approximation, or perhaps it is like a king discussing secret matters, which cannot be done by conspiring with the entire realm, and so forth.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates that a single wholesome mind contains the ten dharma-realms; as these ten realms interact with one another, they contain a hundred dharma-realms and a thousand natures and characteristics. Thus, the ten wholesome acts are themselves the myriad dharmas, and in terms of the Eightfold Noble Path, they comprise the eighty thousand dharma-gates, and so forth.
The phrase "all are non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" clarifies their stage (*avasthā*). *Anuttara* here means "unsurpassed.
The Path is explained as it pertains to the excellence of the object (*viṣaya*), while the stage is explained as it pertains to the excellence of the position (*avasthā*).
Regarding "non-retrogression," it is discussed in terms of stage, practice, and mindfulness, and should be distinguished according to four aspects:
not being born in the three evil realms constitutes non-retrogression in stage;
not being born in a borderland, having all faculties complete, and not receiving a female body constitutes non-retrogression in practice.
To take conventional truth as one's destiny and thus never regress in thought—possessing this is called the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
This is the meaning of the Tripiṭaka.
If it is prior to the sixth mind, the Bodhisattva is like light down; their root of faith has not yet been established, and their status may still regress.

From the seventh mind upward, from the first stage through the sixth stage, one does not regress to the level of an ordinary person or a follower of the two vehicles; this is called non-retrogression in rank and position (*wei-bu-tui*).
Although the active afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, one has not yet been able to universally cultivate the myriad practices, and thus these practices still undergo retrogression.

Upon reaching the seventh stage, it is called non-retrogression in practice (*xing-bu-tui*); yet because one still gives rise to thoughts of the two vehicles, there is retrogression in thought (*nian-tui*).

Upon reaching the eighth stage, the path and contemplation enter into a dual flow, merging into the stream of the Dharma; this is called "non-retrogression through mindfulness" (*smṛty-avivarti*). This is termed the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), which refers to the meaning of the ten stages common to the three vehicles.
The Master of the Stages said:

"The Ten Abodes are non-retrogression through realization; the Ten Practices are non-retrogression in rank; the Ten Dedications are non-retrogression in conduct; and the Ten Grounds are non-retrogression in mindfulness."
This is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddhayāna); it does not accord with this sutra and is therefore not employed here.
The *Āṭānāṭīya-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) states:
"In the first stage (*bhūmi*), the three contemplations manifest before one; moment by moment, they are quiescent and extinguished, naturally flowing into [the ultimate]."
This is also the non-retrogression of the Separate Teaching (pratyeka-śāsana), which is not what is intended here.

If the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that one attains the single body and infinite bodies of a Tathāgata at the first stage (*bhūmi*), possessing the three kinds of non-retrogression—this is the non-retrogression of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This is a single reality; it is by means of this that the stages are now determined.
Regarding the fundamental and the manifested: the fundamental ground of quiescent extinction transcends even the tenth stage, let alone the first dwelling;
it transcends even the non-retrogression of the first dwelling, let alone the Distinct or Shared teachings.

The positions of the Separate and Common Teachings should be used to explain the assemblies listed in other sutras; the position of the Perfect Teaching belongs specifically to the present sutra. Since the masters of various sutras and treatises do not recognize the traces, how can they know the source?
Since what is praised is already erroneous, censure is inherent within it; thus, one ends up committing the two slanders of exaggeration and depreciation. What, then, can be called "praising virtue"?

As for the contemplation of the mind: the three contemplations are themselves the three non-regressions, and furthermore, the three contemplations within a single mind are the three non-regressions within a single mind, and so forth.
The old commentary states:
"All have attained dhāraṇīs" marks the beginning of the praise of virtues (*guṇa-varṇana*).

Here, however, we take "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*) as encompassing both meanings: it completes the preceding section by clarifying the stage (*bhūmi*), and it initiates the subsequent section by belonging to the praise of virtues.
The ancient commentary states: "The praise of virtue consists of twelve phrases, divided into four meanings.

The first three phrases praise present virtues; the next three phrases praise past conduct; the following four phrases praise the internal essence; and the final two phrases praise the external reputation. Although these four meanings differ, virtue occupies the primary position; therefore, it is called 'Praise of Virtue'."
The praise of the present further consists of two parts:
the first line praises his own practice, while the latter two lines praise his transformation of others.
The praise of his conduct is threefold:
The first phrase praises the root of practice; this root is the attainment of *prajñā* from all Buddhas.
The second phrase praises fundamental practice, which is the cultivation of merit; possessing such merit, one is able to support wisdom.
The third phrase describes being praised by the Buddha.
The essence [of the praise] further consists of three parts:

first, the praise of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) through compassion; in the middle, two lines praise the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) of mind and wisdom; and finally, one line praises the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). This praise is twofold:
[the praise of the qualities and the praise of the name].
"The first phrase praises the fame of his name being universally heard; the second phrase praises his ability to deliver sentient beings.
This division of the text is quite clever, yet when scrutinizing the fundamental essence of the doctrine, it lacks any real direction.

If one praises the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the Shared Teaching lacks the three bodies; furthermore, it does not involve entry into the Buddha-wisdom, its name is not universally renowned, and its various meanings are not established.

If one praises the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), since the first stage of the Distinct Teaching already surpasses the two vehicles, why would the thought of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas arise again at the seventh stage?

If one praises the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), one should not say that those from the seventh stage downward lack the virtue of non-retrogression; since such praise and censure would both be inappropriate, in the end, whom is one praising?
This is of no use.

Now, these thirteen phrases are used to analyze the text both horizontally and vertically: first, the vertical arrangement is for the convenience of explaining the meaning of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
second, the horizontal arrangement is for the convenience of explaining the meaning of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).

The term "non-retrogression" (avaivartika) completes the preceding section, which clarifies the stage [of the bodhisattva]; it initiates the subsequent section, which praises his virtues, in contrast to the first bhūmi.

The first bhūmi is named "Joyful" (pramuditā); one rejoices because of not falling back into the two extremes and entering the Middle Way to attain the three kinds of non-retrogression. Thus, we know that this praises the initial Joyful Ground.

"All have attained dhāraṇīs" praises the second bhūmi. The second bhūmi is named "Stainless" (Vimalā) and is also called "Attainment through Separation" (Vimuktidarśana); it is so named because it separates from all evils and attains the upholding of all virtues, which is precisely the meaning of *dhāraṇī*. Therefore, one knows that this praises the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

The "eloquence of joy in teaching" (*pratibhāna*) praises the third stage; the third stage is called the "Stage of Clarity" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). This is because there is internal clarity of wisdom and external eloquence of exposition. One who wishes to know wisdom must look to its expression in speech, and within that speech there are various forms of joy; since this eloquence is the most supreme, it is known that this praises the third stage, the Stage of Clarity.

The phrase "turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma" praises the fourth stage. The fourth stage is named "Blaze" (*jvālā*); a blaze can destroy darkness and also consume the wick. Turning the wheel of Dharma destroys one's own delusions as if consuming a wick, and dispels the confusion of others as if removing darkness; thus, we know this praises the fourth stage, the Blaze.

"Making offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas" praises the fifth stage. The fifth stage is named the "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā). On this stage, one attains profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and by means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one becomes difficult to surpass and difficult to equal; in a single thought-moment, one reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas. Therefore, it is known that this praises the fifth stage.

"Planting the roots of all virtues under the various Buddhas" praises the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*). The sixth stage is named "Manifestation" (*abhimukhī*); because one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is able to make offerings to the Buddhas, whereby merit serves as the support for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). When this knowledge of all modes manifests, that knowledge constitutes the root of virtue. Just as planting a seed in the earth, it is known that this praises the sixth stage.

"Constantly praised by all Buddhas" refers to the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi. Because the skillful means (*upāya*) of the two types of knowledge in this stage transcend all others, and because one extensively cultivates benefit that accords with the Buddha’s mind, it is known that the seventh stage is being praised.

"Refining the body through loving-kindness" praises the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā). Although correct wisdom is immovable and does not emerge from the triple world, one nevertheless governs the body to enter the five realms of existence, governs the mouth to preach the Dharma, and governs the mind to establish skillful means. Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* fully governs these three karmas, we know that this praises the eighth stage.

"Skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom" praises the ninth stage; the ninth stage is named "Excellent Wisdom" (Sādhumatī). Because it penetrates deeply into the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and thoroughly reaches the wondrous source, this name and meaning are most appropriate; thus we know this praises the ninth stage.

"Thoroughly penetrating great wisdom" praises the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). The tenth stage is named "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmameghā*): the *dharmakāya* is like space, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is like a great cloud, and wisdom (*prajñā*) is like a heavy rain. Skillfully entering the Buddha-dharma is called "wisdom," while skillfully applying the Buddha-dharma is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*); these are mentioned alternately.

"Reaching the other shore" praises the internal virtues within the ten stages; it expresses the fruit within the cause of reaching the other shore of the three truths, and it also implies that this arrival will occur before long.

"The renown is universally heard" praises the external virtues beyond the ten stages; because the internal virtues are profound and vast, they cause one's fame to be universally heard, such that the internal and external correspond to one another.
Regarding the phrase "if one awakens to the stage of Perfect Enlightenment," these two lines serve as a comparison.

As for "being able to deliver hundreds of thousands of sentient beings," while those in other stages may deliver people across one realm up to nine realms, this is not termed "being able to deliver"; it is only because the tenth stage is superior to the preceding ones that it is called "being able to deliver."

All the stages (bhūmis) are fully endowed with manifold merits; yet, the reason they now appear and disappear in this commentary on the *Śāstra* is because people’s dispositions favor novelty, for the sake of convenience in designating the ten stages, and because it is easier to understand when the principles are presented vertically; thus, I have composed this single path merely as an exegesis of the text.
Next, regarding the "horizontal praise," this is explained specifically in reference to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*); the other stages may be understood by analogy.

In the first stage of the initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), one resolves for all at once; transcending the two extremes, transforming the ordinary and surpassing the holy, one enters the Middle Way. Because the mind is quiescent and each thought-moment flows into the ocean of *sarvajñatā*, it is said that one attains non-retrogression.

In the first stage (prathamabhūmi), one obstructs and abandons the hindrances of grasping at signs, ignorance, and nescience, while upholding and attaining virtues such as prajñā, liberation, and the dharma-body; therefore, it is said that one "attains dhāraṇī."
Even those at the stage of the ten faiths, who possess only a semblance of understanding, are able to fill the trichiliocosm with sublime sounds; how much more so for those in the first dwelling?
Because the merit of their true understanding and oral secrecy is such, they are said to possess the eloquence of joyful speech.

In the first stage, one is able to manifest as a Buddha in a hundred worlds; in reality, these manifestations are immeasurable and boundless. Because one is thus able to become a Buddha, preach the Dharma, and transform sentient beings, it is said that one can turn the irreversible wheel of the Dharma.

In the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one attains inconceivable supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and is able to serve all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); hence it is said that one makes offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
In this first stage, one attains the root of true reality (*lakṣaṇatattva*) and is able to plant all manner of virtues.
In the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; since this knowledge and vision are identical to those of all Buddhas, one is praised by the Buddhas.

In the first stage, through unconditioned compassion (*nirālambanā maitrī*), one universally manifests the form-body (*rūpakāya*) throughout the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that "one cultivates the body with compassion."
Because one enters the secret treasury at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), it is said that they "skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
Because the threefold wisdom within a single mind is unimpeded at the first stage, it is said that they "penetrate great wisdom."
Because the phenomena and principle of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) are fully perfected, it is said that one has "reached the other shore.
Because the perfect virtues of the first stage are truly in accord with their names, it is said that "one's reputation is heard throughout all Buddha-worlds."

The first stage (prathamā-bhūmi) is able to serve as the basis for the ten dharma-realms and establish their protection; therefore, it is said that one can deliver hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
Furthermore, this first stage possesses immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable varieties of merit, of which only thirteen points have been briefly mentioned.
